newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Mboweni still optimistic on labour deal.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Mboweni still optimistic on labour deal.

text.p: Labour Minister Tito Mboweni said he remained upbeat that sufficient consensus would be reached between business and labour over planned employment legislation by the first of a series of deadlines on Friday.
"Friday is key. I am optimistic that sufficient agreement will be reached in order for us to meet our deadlines," he said on Tuesday.

A series of urgent bilateral meetings were taking place with labour and business ahead of Friday, the deadline set for the parties to at least reach broad consensus if not full agreement on outstanding issues on the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill.
"It's tight but I am not worried. What we are wanting is a basic floor of rights for workers and I am optimistic that we will find each other by Friday," Mboweni said.
Mboweni said broad consensus had to be reached by Friday in order for the bill to be presented to parliament by September 15.
"By Wednesday next week it (the bill) will have to be redrafted and by Thursday it will be circulated to cabinet ministers for consideration."
It would then be passed on to various cabinet committees.
He said there had already been good progress in the majority of provisions proposed in the bill but labour and business remained deadlocked over key clauses.
In terms of one of the key issues -- maternity leave -- parties appeared set to agree terms for the payment of maternity leave benefits out of the state-run Unemployment Insurance Fund.
But business was still unhappy over proposals for increased overtime rates from a minimum of time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half and provisions for three days family responsibility leave.
While business has agreed to a reduction in the working week from 48 to 45 as proposed in the bill, labour wanted a commitment to a 40-hour week within a specific period.

"In terms of working hours we have conducted a study of countries of the same economic development as South Africa and concluded that 45 is within the ballpark of developing countries such as ours," Mboweni said.
The proposed new employment legislation for the first time extends the scope of coverage to vulnerable and low paid workers such as farm and domestic workers.
It covers all workers in the country except soldiers, intelligence service workers and unpaid volunteers. Part-time workers will receive proportional rights and be entitled to annual and maty leave.
